descriptions: the suchness of the Tathāgata and the suchness of all dharmas are one suchness, undivided (Aṣṭasāhasrikā 16)
the Tathāgata is non-arising, the reality-limit, emptiness, suchness — which neither come nor go (Aṣṭa 31)
all dharmas have the mark of emptiness: unborn, unceasing, not defiled, not pure, not deficient, not complete (Heart, s6)
the Tathāgata is to be seen from the dharma; the guides have the dharma for body; dharmatā cannot be cognized (Vajracchedikā 26)
the one buddha-vehicle (Lotus 2); the Tathāgata's lifespan is immeasurable (Lotus 16)
entry into non-duality is Vimalakīrti's silence, where there is no movement of letters, sounds or ideas (Vimalakīrti 8.33)
negations: not the least dharma is found in anuttarā samyaksaṃbodhi — therefore it is called so (Vajracchedikā 22)
even nirvāṇa is like an illusion, like a dream; if there were anything higher than nirvāṇa that too would be like an illusion (Aṣṭa 2)
in emptiness there is no form ... no suffering, origin, cessation, path; no knowing and no attaining (Heart s6-7)
not existent, not non-existent; the middle between 'is' and 'is not' (Kāśyapaparivarta §60)
relation_to_self: Persons and dharmas are both without self (pudgala- and dharma-nairātmya); the bodhisattva who has the notion of a self, a being, a soul or a person is not a bodhisattva (Vajracchedikā 3, 14). Some sūtras nonetheless name the buddha-nature 'self' (see ult:tathagatagarbha).
relation_to_world: The world is empty, dependently arisen, like an illusion, dream or reflection; it is not annihilated either. Form is emptiness and emptiness is form (Heart s4); saṃsāra and nirvāṇa are not two (Vimalakīrti 8); the purity of a buddha-field follows the purity of the mind (Vimalakīrti 1.14).
caveat: The Prajñāpāramitā denies that emptiness, suchness or nirvāṇa is an entity or a substance: they are 'names only', to be neither grasped nor rejected, and 'the view of emptiness' is itself declared incurable (Kāśyapaparivarta §64-65). The sūtras also speak of the Buddha's eternal dharmakāya and of compassionate buddhas and bodhisattvas, which is why 'both' is recorded; they reject any creator god and any reading of suchness as a Brahman-like self (Laṅkāvatāra p. 33, on the tīrthikas' ātman).

names.name: tathāgatagarbha (the embryo / matrix of the Tathāgata)
suchness with stains (samalā tathatā) and without stains (nirmalā tathatā)
the true self (the 'great self', mahātman) of the Mahāparinirvāṇa
the one mind (yixin), in the Awakening of Faith

descriptions: all beings are tathāgatagarbhas: the buddha's knowledge pervades them, suchness is undivided, and the gotra is present (RGV 1.27-28)
the dharmakāya has the perfections of purity, self, bliss and permanence (RGV 1.35; Śrīmālā ch. 12)
empty of the separable adventitious stains, not empty of the inseparable unsurpassed qualities (RGV 1.154-155; Śrīmālā ch. 9)
'self' means the tathāgatagarbha; all beings have buddha-nature (Mahāparinirvāṇa, T374 juan 7)
buddha-nature is the emptiness of the highest meaning, which is wisdom and the middle way (Mahāparinirvāṇa, T374 juan 27)
negations: nothing is to be removed from it and nothing added (RGV 1.154)
not the self of the tīrthikas, but taught to remove the fear of no-self (Laṅkāvatāra, Vaidya p. 33)
relation_to_self: The garbha is the being's own true nature; the Mahāparinirvāṇa and Śrīmālā call it 'self' (the perfection of self), in contrast to the false self imagined in the aggregates. Other readers (Laṅkāvatāra, Madhyamaka) hold that this 'self' language is a skillful means pointing to emptiness.
relation_to_world: Saṃsāra depends on the tathāgatagarbha (Śrīmālā ch. 13), as does nirvāṇa; the defilements are adventitious, like clouds before the sun; beings and buddhas do not differ in the dhātu, only in its being obscured or revealed.
caveat: The tathāgatagarbha texts insist the garbha is not an ātman of the tīrthikas, not a creator, and not separate from emptiness; the tradition divides on whether its permanence and 'self' are definitive (Jonang shentong, many East Asian readings) or provisional (Laṅkāvatāra's own gloss; Gelug). See dsp:buddha-nature-self-or-emptiness and dsp:rangtong-shentong.
